paper_metadata.title: Accelerating variational quantum Monte Carlo using the variational quantum eigensolver

summary: This paper studies quantum-enhanced variational Monte Carlo (QEVMC), where VQE-generated samples are used as the initial distribution for classical VMC. On the Fermi-Hubbard model, the authors report speedups up to 14x in simulated data and up to 6x experimentally for 1x4, while on the transverse-field Ising model they report up to 20x speedup for 16 spins and up to 46x for 24 spins in MCMC/SR convergence. The work does not demonstrate an end-to-end quantum advantage; it shows that better quantum-prepared initial states can accelerate a classical Monte Carlo procedure.

experiments.description: Quantum-enhanced variational Monte Carlo (QEVMC) applied to the Fermi-Hubbard model using VQE-generated initial samples, evaluated on small exact instances and larger scalable instances.

algorithm.variant: VQE-generated initial distribution used to accelerate VMC (QEVMC)

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Computational-basis bitstrings represent fermionic occupation configurations; VMC samples basis states and uses a Metropolis-Hastings mixer that moves an electron to a neighboring site (bit flips 01<->10 within a spin sector).
problem_formulation.objective_function: Minimize the energy of the Fermi-Hubbard Hamiltonian using the Gutzwiller wavefunction within VMC, with VQE samples used as the initial distribution.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Implicit physical-occupancy constraints via the mixer and postselection/error mitigation in the experimental VQE distributions; no explicit penalty formulation reported.
problem_formulation.problem_hamiltonian: H = - sum_{<i,j>,sigma}(a^†_{iσ} a_{jσ} + a^†_{jσ} a_{iσ}) + U sum_k n_{k↑} n_{k↓}

problem_instance.description: Fermi-Hubbard model instances at half-filling, including small benchmark systems and larger 1xL systems for scalability.
problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Experimental VQE distributions were error-mitigated by postselection on occupation number and averaging over time-reversal and reflection symmetries.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Total variation distance to target distribution, local energy / energy error, and speedup factor measured as ratio of Metropolis chain lengths needed to reach a given TVD; larger systems evaluated via mean energy over 10,000 runs.

noise_model.noise_type: experimental hardware noise; postselection and symmetry averaging used as mitigation
noise_model.error_mitigation_method: postselection on occupation number; averaging over time-reversal and reflection symmetries

implementation_details.mitigation_details: Experimental distributions were postselected on occupation number and symmetrized by time-reversal and reflection averaging.
implementation_details.classical_solver: Metropolis-Hastings VMC / exact stochastic matrix multiplication for small instances
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Energy estimated from local energy averages; speedup computed from chain-length ratios.

speedup_claims.conditions: simulated VQE distribution for 1x8 Fermi-Hubbard instance; speedup defined as ratio of Metropolis chain lengths needed to reach a given total variation distance
speedup_claims.caveats: Speedup depends on target TVD threshold; experimental 1x8 and 2x4 cases showed little speedup.

speedup_claims.conditions: experimental VQE distribution for 1x4 Fermi-Hubbard instance; chain-length ratio to reach a given total variation distance
speedup_claims.caveats: Based on experimental distributions with postselection and symmetry averaging.

speedup_claims.conditions: experimental VQE distributions for 1x8 and 2x4 Fermi-Hubbard instances
speedup_claims.caveats: Paper states there is little speedup obtained in these experiments.

speedup_claims.conditions: 1x16, 1x24, 1x48 VMC runs using concatenated 1x8 VQE samples
speedup_claims.caveats: Total variation distance is not accessible for large system sizes, so the effect is assessed via energy convergence only.

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not established; reported speedups are up to 14x in simulated VQE and up to 6x in 1x4 experimental data, but not consistently across all instances.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Offline access to VQE-generated samples; classical Metropolis-Hastings VMC; no data-loading bottleneck beyond sample transfer/storage is analyzed.
limiting_factors: Speedup is only for MCMC convergence from a better initial distribution, not end-to-end wall-clock advantage
Experimental speedup is inconsistent across 1x8 and 2x4 cases
Classical VMC remains the main solver and can reproduce the same objective
No asymptotic quantum advantage or complexity separation is shown

notes: Hardware is inferred to be a real superconducting QPU because the paper cites experimental VQE data from Stanisic et al. (2021) on quantum hardware, but does not name the device in this paper.
No explicit qubit count is given for the Fermi-Hubbard VQE experiments; the paper only states the larger VMC runs use up to 96 qubits in the classical scaling study by concatenating 1x8 samples.
The paper reports faster convergence to the target distribution and lower energy in some cases, but does not demonstrate a practical end-to-end quantum advantage over classical methods.

experiments.description: Quantum-enhanced variational Monte Carlo (QEVMC) applied to the transverse-field Ising model using VQE-generated initial samples, evaluated on exact small systems, larger VMC runs, and stochastic reconfiguration acceleration.

algorithm.variant: Hamiltonian variational ansatz used to generate initial samples for VMC / SR

hyperparameters.energy_estimation_window: last 5 iterations (or last 10 points for one estimate)

algorithm.parameter_initialization: VQE parameters optimized from the all-plus state; initial NQS weights chosen randomly for the SR baseline.

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Spin configurations are represented as computational-basis bitstrings; VMC samples bitstrings and estimates local energy from them.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Minimize the energy of the transverse-field Ising Hamiltonian using an NQS target state, with VQE samples used as the initial distribution for MCMC.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: No explicit constraints beyond the MCMC proposal rule (single-spin flips) and the NQS/VMC sampling procedure.
problem_formulation.problem_hamiltonian: H = -J sum_{i=1}^{N-1} Z_i Z_{i+1} - h sum_{j=1}^{N} X_j

problem_instance.description: 1D transverse-field Ising model in open boundary conditions for the VQE-generated samples; larger NQS comparisons also use 40- and 80-spin systems.

dataset_specification.boundary_conditions: open boundary conditions for the VQE-generated 20-spin samples used in stitching; original NQS reference includes periodic boundary conditions

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: For larger systems, 20-spin VQE samples are concatenated independently to form initial samples for 40- and 80-spin systems.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Exact total variation distance and energy error for 16 spins; local energy error for 24 spins; relative energy error for 40/80 spins; speedup measured by chain-length ratio and SR-iteration ratio.

noise_model.noise_type: experimental hardware noise; no explicit noise model reported

implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Local energy averaging over 5000 samples; relative error computed against exact or estimated ground-state energy; speedup factors computed from chain-length or iteration counts.

results.unit: x (24-spin SR, VQE vs uniform; approximate from figure)
relative error for 24-spin NQS estimate (300 iterations)

speedup_claims.conditions: 16-spin TFI, h = 1, using a four-layer VQE state as the initial distribution for MCMC toward an already trained NQS
speedup_claims.caveats: Speedup measured by chain-length ratio to reach a given TVD; exact distributions used.

speedup_claims.conditions: 24-spin TFI, h = 1, using a one-layer VQE state as the initial distribution for MCMC toward an already trained NQS
speedup_claims.caveats: Speedup measured using local-energy estimates rather than exact TVD for the 24-spin case.

speedup_claims.conditions: 40- and 80-spin TFI systems using stitched 20-spin VQE samples
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper states the speedup scales up with system size, but does not provide a single numeric factor for all cases.

speedup_claims.factor: higher speedup with more VQE layers
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper reports that more VQE layers allow higher speedup, but does not give a single numeric factor for each layer in text.

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not established; reported speedups reach up to 20x for 16 spins and up to 46x for 24 spins in MCMC/SR convergence, but no end-to-end advantage is shown.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Offline VQE sample generation, then classical MCMC/SR; 5000 samples per energy estimate; 3 parameters per VQE layer and up to 4 layers.
limiting_factors: Speedup is in initialization of classical Monte Carlo, not a full quantum algorithmic speedup
No hardware-scale or fault-tolerant regime analysis
No asymptotic complexity advantage is proven
Results depend on using VQE samples as a better starting distribution

notes: Hardware is inferred to be a real superconducting QPU because the paper cites experimental VQE data from prior quantum-hardware experiments, but no device name is given here.
The paper reports up to four VQE layers and three parameters per layer, but does not state the total qubit count for the VQE circuits in this paper.
The paper shows reduced MCMC chain length and faster SR convergence when seeded with VQE samples, but this is not a demonstrated quantum advantage in the Hoefler sense.
